podcast.title: All-Female Formation in San Francisco (1967)
podcast.body: Ace of Cups formed as an all-female rock band consisting of five women in San Francisco in 1967, coinciding with the Summer of Love. This was a groundbreaking concept at a time when all-female rock bands were virtually unheard of. "They were formed in San Francisco in 1967, right in time for the summer of love."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Female Rock Band (1967)
podcast.body: An all-female rock band from San Francisco that wrote their own songs, had a frontwoman who could "shred like a man," and a female drummer. This lineup was considered radical even in 1967, challenging prevailing norms about women in rock music. "An all-girl rock band? A bunch of women who wrote their own songs, went a checkout front that could shred like a man and a girl playing drums? Even in 1967, this was radical."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup Due to Sexism (1972)
podcast.body: Despite their talent and early recognition, the band broke up by 1972, attributed to the re-emergence of old sexist attitudes in the music industry that dismissed the idea of female rock bands. "The Ace of Cups gave it a good shot, but by 1972, they'd broken up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lack of Professional Recordings and Breakup (1972)
podcast.body: Ace of Cups never released any professional recordings during their active years, as initial record deals ultimately did not materialize. The band eventually broke up in 1972 after a couple of members became parents and were replaced by male musicians. "The ace of cups never did make any professional recordings. Record deals didn't really come through."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: All-Female San Francisco Group
podcast.body: Ace of Cups was an all-female group formed in San Francisco in 1967, featuring Diane Metilige on drums. They were noted for opening for Jimi Hendrix and maintaining friendships with prominent bands like Jefferson Airplane and The Grateful Dead, marking their presence in the late 1960s psychedelic rock scene. "They were at all-female group formed in 1967 and featured die-end metallige on drums."

podcast.title: Altamont Festival Incident
podcast.body: During the Altamont Festival in December 1969, one of the band members suffered a fractured skull after being hit by a full beer can, requiring brain surgery. "Another issue happened when one of the band members suffered a fractured skull when she was hit by a full beer can during the awful Altamont Festival in December 1969."

podcast.title: Associated with Influential Bay Area Bands
podcast.body: The band were friends with other prominent San Francisco bands of the era, including the Grateful Dead and the Jefferson Airplane, demonstrating their integration into the vibrant local music scene. "They were also friends with the great full dead in the Jefferson Airplane and the guys in the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup and Posthumous Release
podcast.body: The band broke up in 1972 after a couple of members became parents and were replaced by men. They had been poised to be the first all-female rock band to release a record, but this did not happen until a CD of their demos and live tracks was released in 2003. "It wasn't until 2003 that a CD of demos and live tracks was released."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Early Connections
podcast.body: Formed in San Francisco in 1967, coinciding with the Summer of Love, Ace of Cups consisted of five women without any male members. They were friends with The Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane, and Jimi Hendrix was so impressed that he invited them to open one of his gigs at Golden Gate Park. "They were formed in San Francisco in 1967, right in time for the summer of love."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jimmy Hendrix's Support
podcast.body: Jimi Hendrix was greatly impressed by the band's musical talent and invited them to open for a couple of his shows, signaling a significant early endorsement for the all-female group. "Hendrix was so impressed by their chops that he invited them to open a couple of his shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Potential First All-Female Album
podcast.body: The band was poised to make a groundbreaking impact as potentially the first all-female rock band to release a record, but this never came to fruition during their initial run. Their unreleased material was ahead of its time, sounding similar to modern indie rock. "They could have been the first ever all-female rock band to release a record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Record Deal Amidst Sexism
podcast.body: Despite the prevalent sexism of the 1960s, Ace of Cups managed to secure a record deal. However, they were "low balled" on the value of their contracts, explicitly because they were women, highlighting the discriminatory practices they faced in the industry. "They did get a record deal despite the rampant sexism of the era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sexism and Lack of Professional Releases
podcast.body: Despite securing a record deal, the band experienced rampant sexism, receiving low-balled contract offers because they were women. They ultimately never made any professional recordings, and their record deals failed to materialize. "They did get a record deal despite the rampant sexism of the era. Although they were low balled on the value of these contracts because they were only women."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

The severe injury necessitated brain surgery, highlighting the dangerous environment of the festival. concerts.title: Golden Gate Park (Opening for Jimi Hendrix)
concerts.body: Jimi Hendrix, impressed by Ace of Cups, personally invited them to open one of his gigs at Golden Gate Park. This was a significant opportunity for the all-female band, showcasing their talent to a large audience. "Jimmy Hendrix saw what they were doing and invited them to open one of his gigs at Golden Gate Park."
